claims.text: The initial eutectic high-entropy alloy has dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries.
Phase-selective recrystallization can improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility relative to as-cast or fully recrystallized eutectic high-entropy alloys.
Phase-selective recrystallization eliminates weak internal boundaries.
Eliminating weak boundaries prevents premature crack nucleation.
The relevant performance is measured by quasi-static uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature.
Phase-selective recrystallization produces a skeletal, non-recrystallized B2 phase together with a recrystallized FCC phase.
The recrystallized FCC and non-recrystallized B2 phases contribute simultaneously to strain hardening.
High-density dislocation multiplication contributes to strain hardening in the phase-selectively recrystallized alloy.
A strain-induced B2-to-BCT phase transformation contributes to strain hardening.
The phase-selectively recrystallized alloy can achieve a uniform elongation of approximately 33%.
The phase-selectively recrystallized alloy can achieve an engineering ultimate tensile strength approaching 2.2 GPa.
As-cast and fully recrystallized baselines have lower ductility than the phase-selectively recrystallized alloy.
As-cast and fully recrystallized baselines have lower tensile strength than the phase-selectively recrystallized alloy.
The effectiveness of phase-selective recrystallization is limited to eutectic high-entropy alloys having a specific, but unspecified, microstructure.
The applicability of phase-selective recrystallization to other alloy systems remains to be established.
The exact mechanisms and property effects of phase-selective recrystallization are not fully understood.
